rationale: Block 4 covers the neuroanatomy of referred otalgia. Testing knowledge of which cranial nerve mediates referred otalgia from the tonsillar fossa addresses a high-yield EN known-trap about correctly identifying the nerve basis of referred pain.

Block 7 covers differential diagnosis of otalgia. A normal otoscopy in an adult with otalgia must never be dismissed as psychosomatic — this is an EN known-trap (the most dangerous error in otalgia management).

Block 3 covers clinical presentation of external ear diseases. Malignant otitis externa (MOE) is the most dangerous EAC condition and the EN known-trap here is that severity of pain is disproportionate to early otoscopic appearance — a critical diagnostic clue.

Block 9 covers principles of management. The EN known-trap for malignant OE is the need for prolonged anti-pseudomonal therapy and the futility of topical drops alone; this question tests correct management priority.

Block 4 covers anatomy and pathophysiology of ear discharge. The CSOM safe/unsafe (tubotympanic vs atticoantral) distinction is the central EN known-trap for ear discharge — atticoantral disease carries cholesteatoma risk and requires surgery, not topical drops.

Block 7 covers diagnosis and differential diagnosis, specifically classifying CSOM as tubotympanic (safe) vs atticoantral (unsafe). This question tests the key distinguishing features used to make this critical classification.

Block 6 covers procedure and technique for wax removal. An EN known-trap is that syringing is absolutely contraindicated with a history of TM perforation, mastoid surgery, or previous ear surgery — this question tests correct contraindication recognition.

Block 8 covers interpretation of findings after wax removal. Recognising that wax removal must end with a TM assessment — and that a newly revealed perforation changes subsequent management — is a key clinical competency.
